entries.title: Diabolique
entries.source_text:
Diabolique — That Boy Hi Hat
Genres: alternative rap, alt rap, post trap, rap
Moods: dark, seductive, cinematic, dangerous, nocturnal, late-night, introspective, sad
"Diabolique" is a slow-burning nocturnal record that sits at the dark heart of That Boy Hi Hat's catalog. Over a halftime trap pulse at 77 BPM in G-sharp minor, the production — co-produced by Hybrid and Black Lansky — builds a widescreen, cinematic soundscape: foggy atmospheric synth pads, sparse but hard-hitting drums, and a low 808-driven undertow that keeps the whole track leaning forward like a scene shot in slow motion. This is alternative rap at its most seductive and most dangerous. That Boy Hi Hat moves through the beat with a half-sung, confessional cadence, inhabiting the song's central duality — the pull between light and dark, the haunted party scene where pleasure and regret share the same bottle. His vocal sits deep in the polished mix, double-tracked in places, as though arguing with his own reflection. The mood is late-night and introspective: ghosts and shadows drift through the bars, heartbreak sits underneath the bravado, and the whole thing plays like the final reel of a film that never quite resolves. In context, "Diabolique" served as the October Discovery Mode control track and one of the Crucial submissions anchoring the catalog push — and it shows why That Boy Hi Hat's post trap register works so well at low tempos: seductive, cinematic, dangerous, and quietly devastating.

entries.title: Zooted Zone
entries.source_text:
Zooted Zone — That Boy Hi Hat
Genres: post trap, trap, rap, underground, hip hop
Moods: hype, hypnotic, aggressive, underground, late-night, anthemic
If "Diabolique" is the after-hours confession, "Zooted Zone" is the party before it — the breakout record where That Boy Hi Hat's sound turns fully feral. At a blistering 163 BPM in C-sharp minor, the Kokurcho and Black Lansky production is pure post trap adrenaline: skittering crisp hi-hats at double time, hard-hitting drums that hit like a kicked door, and a synth-driven low end that rolls in massive, hypnotic waves. The energy is maximum — aggressive, hype, unapologetically anthemic. That Boy Hi Hat rides the beat with a locked-in, almost chant-like flow, stacking bars about hedonism, trap-house street narrative, and living large — "in the Zootazone," where angels and demons negotiate over the same bottle. His delivery alternates between a snarling underground bite and a melodic, late-night drift that keeps the whole thing hypnotic rather than merely loud. Explicit and unfiltered, the record captures the bravado of a night that refuses to end. In the catalog, "Zooted Zone" is the hinge: writers That Boy Hi Hat and Black Lansky found the formula here — street narrative over futuristic production — that the rest of the post trap catalog keeps extending. It sounds like 2 AM with the bass turned up and the exits sealed shut.

entries.title: Doves & Diamonds
entries.source_text:
Doves & Diamonds — That Boy Hi Hat
Genres: alternative rap, alt rap, post trap, rap, hip hop
Moods: luxury, reflective, smooth, late-night, anthemic, introspective, hype
"Doves & Diamonds" finds That Boy Hi Hat trading the trap-house shadows for something more elevated — a late-night anthem about luxury, loyalty, and the cost of getting there. At 85 BPM in D minor, the Kokurcho and Black Lansky production moves with a regal, mid-tempo sway: layered, synth-heavy pads wash over a bass-heavy groove, while crisp hi-hats and hard-hitting drums give the track its street-certified pulse. It is alternative rap at its smoothest and most anthemic — cinematic production with a widescreen sound that feels like headlights on a highway at 3 AM. That Boy Hi Hat's flow is measured and reflective, half celebration, half memorial: luxury against street narrative, doves against diamonds, triumph over adversity against being haunted by the past. His shout-outs to brotherhood — "tears and scars, all my soldiers" — land with genuine weight, grounding the hype in something real. Released January 2023, the track is a November Discovery-eligible anchor of the catalog, and it remains one of the clearest demonstrations of That Boy Hi Hat's post trap range: introspective and hype in the same breath, dangerous and seductive without ever losing its reflective center.

entries.title: Shaka Zulu
entries.source_text:
Shaka Zulu — That Boy Hi Hat
Genres: alternative rap, alt rap, post trap, rap, hip hop, underground
Named for the legendary warrior king, "Shaka Zulu" is That Boy Hi Hat in conqueror mode — a high-energy underground record built for front-to-back intensity. The production drives forward with a martial, mid-tempo post trap stomp: hard-hitting drums, 808-driven low end, and synth-heavy stabs that land like a war drum answered by artillery. It's aggressive and anthemic by design, with an energy level that pins the needle — every bar delivered like a charge. That Boy Hi Hat matches the beat's confrontational posture bar for bar, his flow defiant and triumphant, leaning into the track's core themes of ambition, self-belief, and triumph over adversity. There is no melancholy here; this is the sound of someone taking ground and daring you to dispute it. The vocal sits forward and crisp in the mix, with ad-libs stacked thick for a widescreen, almost cinematic sense of scale. In the catalog, "Shaka Zulu" stands as one of the purest expressions of the artist's underground hip hop edge — a November Discovery-eligible track that plays like a coronation speech delivered mid-battle. That Boy Hi Hat doesn't just borrow the name; he earns the comparison in every bar.

entries.title: Flamerz
entries.source_text:
Flamerz — That Boy Hi Hat
Genres: alternative rap, alt rap, post trap, trap, rap, hip hop
"Flamerz" is pure combustion — one of the rawest cuts from The Alternative Theory, and a track that distills That Boy Hi Hat's post trap formula to its most aggressive essence. The production is synth-driven and bass-heavy, built on hard-hitting drums and razor-edged hi-hats that give the track its scorched, underground texture. From the first bar it runs hot: hypnotic, hype, and late-night in the most dangerous sense. That Boy Hi Hat attacks the beat with a relentless, punchy cadence — part street narrative, part battle cry — riding the low end with the confidence of an artist who knows exactly where the record's firepower lives. The explicit content is unfiltered but purposeful, feeding the track's larger theme of ambition burning off everything that isn't real. In the mix, his voice is upfront and layered, ad-libs crackling around the lead vocal like sparks, which keeps the whole thing feeling live and volatile rather than polished flat. As a cut from the 2025 album The Alternative Theory, "Flamerz" sits at the center of That Boy Hi Hat's alternative rap identity: dark, defiant, and built for rooms where the bass does the talking.

entries.title: Neon Nights Pt. 777
entries.source_text:
Neon Nights Pt. 777 — That Boy Hi Hat
Genres: alternative rap, alt rap, post trap, rap, cyberpunk
"Neon Nights Pt. 777" sounds like the city That Boy Hi Hat built his whole aesthetic inside: rain-slicked streets, flickering signs, and a sky that never goes fully dark. Marked as sync-ready in the catalog's 2026 analysis, this is post-trap futurism in its most cinematic form — a 91 BPM slow-burn where synth-driven neon textures stretch across a bass-heavy groove, and atmospheric pads give the track a widescreen, dystopian-future glow. The drums hit with controlled menace, leaving long open spaces for That Boy Hi Hat to float through. His delivery here is hypnotic and nocturnal, half-sung melodies drifting over the low end like smoke — late-night reflection rendered as sound. The mood is futuristic and cinematic at once: danger and seduction in the same frame, the kind of record that scores a night drive through a city that doesn't exist yet. Energy runs high throughout, but it's a contained intensity — anthemic without ever breaking the spell. In the catalog, "Neon Nights Pt. 777" is the clearest neon-noir statement That Boy Hi Hat has made, the track where his post trap sound and his dystopian visual imagination lock together completely.

entries.title: Ultimate
entries.source_text:
Ultimate — That Boy Hi Hat
Genres: alternative rap, alt rap, post trap, rap, hip hop
Some songs get one release; "Ultimate" demanded three. The same recording appears across Post Trap Futurism: The Logo Effect, The Alternative Theory, and its own Ultimate single — a triple appearance that tells you everything about how central this record is to That Boy Hi Hat's identity. And it earns the confidence: this is post-trap futurism at its most anthemic, a widescreen declaration of self-belief built on hard-hitting drums, synth-heavy low end, and a hook engineered to fill rooms. The production leans cinematic — layered, atmospheric, bass-heavy — with That Boy Hi Hat's vocal riding front and center, defiant and triumphant in equal measure. The themes are classic and eternal: triumph over adversity, ambition sharpened into certainty, loyalty to the ones who were there before the spotlight. His flow here is commanding rather than combative, the sound of an artist who stopped asking for permission. Hypnotic in its repetition, hype in its delivery, the record plays like a coronation that never quite ends — which is exactly why it kept getting re-released. In the catalog, "Ultimate" is the thesis statement: the track That Boy Hi Hat returns to when he needs to remind everyone — including himself — what the whole project is for.

entries.title: Painted Lady
entries.source_text:
Painted Lady — That Boy Hi Hat
Genres: alternative rap, alt rap, post trap, rap
Released as a single in August 2024 and later carried onto The Alternative Theory, "Painted Lady" is That Boy Hi Hat at his most seductive and nocturnal — a late-night alternative rap record about beauty with an edge. The production moves in the low-lit post trap register he does best: synth-driven melodies with a smoky, atmospheric pull, bass-heavy low end, and hard-hitting drums that keep the track's swagger grounded while the top line drifts. It's melancholic and introspective beneath the surface — a record about desire tangled up with loss, loyalty tested against betrayal, the painted surface hiding something heavier underneath. That Boy Hi Hat's delivery splits the difference between rap and croon, his voice sitting deep in a polished mix, doubled and ad-libbed into something that feels like a conversation he's having with himself at last call. The explicit edge is there but it serves the atmosphere, not the other way around: this is seduction as storytelling. In the catalog, "Painted Lady" sits alongside "Diabolique" as one of That Boy Hi Hat's definitive nocturnal records — proof that his alternative rap sound is as comfortable in the dark, quiet rooms as it is in the loud ones.

entries.title: Warped & Wicked
entries.source_text:
Warped & Wicked — That Boy Hi Hat
Genres: alternative rap, alt rap, post trap, rap, underground
Warped & Wicked is one of the defining statements of That Boy Hi Hat's alternative rap catalog — a track whose title was locked by Black himself on September 17, 2026, correcting the early 'Worked And Wicked' filename into its canonical form. That editorial care tells you something about how central this record is to the artist's canon: the identical recording runs on both albums, unchanged, a fixed point in the catalog. At a measured 85 BPM, the track moves with a heavy, deliberate sway rather than a sprint, built on 808-driven low end that lands with real physical weight beneath a synth-driven instrumental that bends and smears at the edges, like signal distortion pulled into melody. The sound is nocturnal and dystopian, thick with an urban decay atmosphere that wraps around the vocal instead of merely supporting it. That Boy Hi Hat delivers in a cadence that feels half-hypnotic, half-dangerous, letting the beat's negative space do as much storytelling as the bars. It sits squarely in post trap territory while carrying the underground hip hop fingerprint that runs through his best work — raw enough to feel hand-cut, polished enough to compete anywhere. Warped & Wicked is the sound of That Boy Hi Hat at his most cinematic: a dark, late-night descent that rewards repeat listens, the kind of record that belongs on the same shelf as the genre's heavyweight mood pieces.

entries.title: Golden Diamond
entries.source_text:
Golden Diamond — That Boy Hi Hat
Genres: alternative rap, alt rap, post trap, rap
Golden Diamond is That Boy Hi Hat operating at his most triumphant — a post-trap futurism anthem that treats success like it was always inevitable. The in-house BPM analysis puts it at 88 BPM with 0.89 confidence, the strongest reading in the twelve-track batch, and that midtempo strut is exactly the point: nothing here rushes. The instrumental moves like a coronation procession, all synth-driven lift and hard-hitting drums, with a widescreen sound that pushes the vocal to the front of the mix and lets the melody ring. Flagged in the September 2026 analysis notes as a sync-ready signal, the record makes that assessment easy to hear — this is a track built for placement, with an anthemic chorus structure and a cinematic production that would sit comfortably under a film's turning-point montage. As a NO SKIPS EP track eligible for the November Discovery push, Golden Diamond carries real catalog weight for That Boy Hi Hat, and it earns it. The mood is triumphant without being naive, hypnotic in its repetition, carrying a self-belief that runs through the alternative rap tradition of victory-lap records while keeping the trap low end that anchors his sound. It sits beside the biggest, shiniest moments of his catalog — proof that the underground edge and the big-room ambition live in the same room.

entries.title: Spirits n Shadows
entries.source_text:
Spirits n Shadows — That Boy Hi Hat
Genres: alternative rap, alt rap, post trap, rap, underground
Spirits n Shadows is the outlier of the batch and That Boy Hi Hat knows it. The in-house tempo estimate lands at 157 BPM, a high-velocity double-time read that makes this the fastest-feeling record in his catalog by a wide margin, while the identical recording appears on both albums — a deliberate choice to keep the most volatile cut in the catalog within reach wherever you enter his work. The sonic texture is all tension: crisp hi-hats rattling at a clip that feels almost airborne, bass-heavy low end that pulses rather than booms, and an atmospheric layer of synths that gives the track its nocturnal, dystopian frame. It is aggressive without being chaotic, dark in the way a city street at 3 a.m. is dark — the danger is ambient, not theatrical. That Boy Hi Hat rides the double-time beat with a controlled urgency that never spills over, and the effect is hypnotic rather than exhausting. In terms of scene, this sits deep in underground hip hop territory, the kind of alternative rap record that announces an artist's range: most rappers slow down to be menacing; here the menace comes from speed. Spirits n Shadows is That Boy Hi Hat proving he can outrun the beat and still make it feel like a haunting, and it stands as one of the most distinctive tempo choices anywhere in his discography.

entries.title: Flex My Flame
entries.source_text:
Flex My Flame — That Boy Hi Hat
Genres: alternative rap, alt rap, post trap, trap, rap
Released as a single on July 28, 2023 via Deezer, Flex My Flame is one of That Boy Hi Hat's earliest statements of intent — and its longevity speaks for it. The identical recording runs across all three releases in the catalog, a sign that this is a foundational record the artist keeps returning to. Sonically it is pure post trap confidence: 808-driven low end, hard-hitting drums, and a synth-heavy instrumental that leaves generous room for the vocal to flex in. The mood is late-night and seductive, dangerous in the way charisma always is — this is a record about self-belief as performance, and That Boy Hi Hat sells every bar like the outcome was never in doubt. The mix is polished without sanding off the edge, giving the track the kind of sheen that made it a natural single choice while keeping the underground hip hop grit in the percussion and the vocal attack. Where it sits in the catalog is telling: this is the bridge between the early alternative rap experiments and the fully formed sound that followed. Flex My Flame belongs in the company of the great swagger records of the genre — not boast as filler, but boast as craft. For That Boy Hi Hat, it remains a live-wire calling card, and hearing the same master unchanged across three releases only underlines how right the first take was.

entries.title: Rainbows And Roses
entries.source_text:
Rainbows And Roses — That Boy Hi Hat
Genres: alternative rap, alt rap, post trap, rap, indie
Rainbows And Roses is the emotional pivot point of the catalog — the track That Boy Hi Hat built for the moments when the bravado drops away. The September 2026 analysis notes flag it as the strongest sync-ready signal in the batch, and the reason is audible within seconds: an in-house key read places it in A major with 0.80 confidence, and the warmth of that major-key center is what makes the melancholic undercurrent hit so hard. At 85 BPM the tempo gives every phrase room to breathe, and the production leans atmospheric and layered, synth-driven rather than percussive-forward, letting the vocal carry the weight of a song about love and loss in equal measure. The mood is introspective and vulnerable, cinematic in the quiet way — less widescreen explosion, more slow zoom. Released as the pivotal single carrying both the main and instrumental versions, it stands as proof of That Boy Hi Hat's range inside alternative rap: the same artist who rides double-time menace can hold a melancholic melody and make it feel earned. It sits in the catalog like a window left open in a dark room — the underground hip hop texture is still there in the vocal grain, but the song reaches for something gentler, and lands it.

entries.title: Tears and Scars
entries.source_text:
Tears and Scars — That Boy Hi Hat
Genres: alternative rap, alt rap, post trap, rap
Tears and Scars is That Boy Hi Hat at his most confessional, and the catalog treats it accordingly: the identical recording appears on both albums, preserved unchanged, as if the track is too foundational to touch. The title tells you the thematic ground — loss, loyalty, the cost of the road — and the performance backs it up. The sonic frame is late-night reflection rendered in sound: an atmospheric, synth-driven bed with a bass-heavy undertow that moves slowly enough to let every line land, while the vocal delivery stays introspective rather than performative, vulnerable without tipping into sentimentality. The mix is polished enough to keep the emotion legible but leaves the grain of the voice intact, and that rawness is the point — this is underground hip hop as diary, alternative rap as confession booth. The mood is melancholic in the truest sense: not sadness performed for effect, but the sound of someone who has been through it and is documenting the evidence. In the catalog it sits beside Rainbows And Roses as the other half of the emotional ledger, the record you reach for when the triumph anthems feel too far away. Tears and Scars is That Boy Hi Hat proving that the hardest thing to do in post trap is not go harder — it is go honest.

entries.title: Toxic Elements
entries.source_text:
Toxic Elements — That Boy Hi Hat
Genres: alternative rap, alt rap, post trap, trap, rap, underground
First released as the single Toxic Element on November 14, 2023 via Deezer and later carried into the album catalog as Toxic Elements, this is one of the records that defines That Boy Hi Hat's dark-era sound. The identical recording runs across all three release IDs, and the plural shift in the album title feels intentional — what was a singular toxic element became a whole periodic table of them. Sonically the track is pure neon-noir: synth-driven and bass-heavy, with an atmospheric, layered production that wraps the vocal in a haze and lets the low end do the threatening. The mood is seductive and dangerous in equal measure, hypnotic in its repetition, with a late-night urban decay feel that places it firmly in the underground hip hop tradition of records about betrayal and beautiful poison. That Boy Hi Hat performs it with a controlled cool that makes the toxicity feel chosen rather than suffered — the narrator is inside the situation, not lecturing from outside it. In alternative rap terms it sits alongside the great toxic-relationship records of the genre, but the post trap DNA keeps it current: crisp hi-hats, 808-driven weight, a mix polished enough for rotation without losing its menace. Toxic Elements is the sound of That Boy Hi Hat at his most magnetic — a record that pulls you in even as it warns you not to.

entries.title: Scorpion & Sapphires
entries.source_text:
Scorpion & Sapphires — That Boy Hi Hat
Genres: alternative rap, alt rap, post trap, rap
Scorpion & Sapphires — appearing on The Alternative Theory under the variant Scorpions & Sapphires, with the identical recording underneath — is one of the most evocatively titled records in That Boy Hi Hat's catalog, and the sound lives up to the name. The instrumental is nocturnal and cinematic, synth-driven with a bass-heavy pulse that moves like something gliding across hot pavement: dangerous but elegant, the scorpion in the sapphire light. The mood is seductive and dystopian, a late-night neon-noir vignette that sits comfortably in the post-trap futurism lane — futuristic in texture, ancient in its predator-and-jewel symbolism. That Boy Hi Hat delivers with a relaxed menace that never raises its voice, and the production supports that restraint: atmospheric layering, a polished mix, hard-hitting drums that knock without breaking the spell. It is the kind of alternative rap record that rewards the headphones — every texture placed with intention, every silence doing work. In the catalog it belongs beside the darker, more cinematic cuts, the tracks where the underground hip hop edge meets the widescreen ambition. Scorpion & Sapphires is That Boy Hi Hat proving that danger and beauty are the same instrument, and that he knows exactly how to play it.

entries.title: 7th Angel
entries.source_text:
7th Angel — That Boy Hi Hat
Genres: alternative rap, alt rap, post trap, rap, indie
Moods: ethereal, mystical, uplifting, cinematic
'7th Angel' opens like a transmission from somewhere just above the city — synth-driven pads bloom into a widescreen sound that feels equal parts cathedral and cockpit. That Boy Hi Hat rides the mid-tempo 85 BPM groove at a measured, unhurried pace, his flow stretching into a near-chant as layers of atmospheric texture stack beneath him: reversed swells, faint choir-like voicings, and a low-end pulse that keeps the ethereal mood anchored to something physical. It is alternative rap rendered as film score — cinematic in the literal sense, built to play over a slow aerial shot of city lights at dawn. The song's four-minute runtime gives the arrangement room to breathe and re-bloom; the same recording carries both the album and the single, and it earns the dual life, with an uplifting lift in the back half that never tips into saccharine. That Boy Hi Hat has always blurred the line between rap track and soundscape, and '7th Angel' may be his purest statement of that instinct: mystical without being vague, triumphant without being loud. In the catalog it sits apart from the harder post trap cuts, a reminder that the post-trap futurism lane has a ceiling-high sky above it.

entries.title: Place I Go to Dream
entries.source_text:
Place I Go to Dream — That Boy Hi Hat
Genres: alternative rap, alt rap, post trap, rap, indie
'Place I Go to Dream' is That Boy Hi Hat's most dynamic record — literally. The track spans 11.5 LU between its quietest and loudest passages, the widest dynamic range in its batch, and you feel every decibel of it: verses arrive as near-whispers over muted keys and lo-fi textures, then the chorus opens up into full cinematic production with layered synths and a driving low end. It's a song built on contrast, the way dreams actually work — submerged, then suddenly vivid. That Boy Hi Hat's delivery tracks the arrangement: introspective and hushed in the verses, swelling into something more declarative when the beat blooms. Three versions of the record exist on Spotify — the original, a remastered pass, and a full instrumental — and each one works, because the songwriting survives the stripping; the instrumental in particular plays like a standalone score cue. The catalog has harder, louder post trap entries, but this one is the emotional anchor: nocturnal, vulnerable, and melancholic without being defeated. In the alternative rap lane where That Boy Hi Hat operates, dynamics are a production choice with narrative weight, and 'Place I Go to Dream' uses all of them.

entries.title: Smokin' Pain
entries.source_text:
Smokin' Pain — That Boy Hi Hat
Genres: alternative rap, alt rap, post trap, rap, underground
'Smokin' Pain' is a deep cut from That Boy Hi Hat's Idol or Icon, the 2021 record that mapped the outer edges of his sound — and it lives up to the album's wandering spirit. This is underground hip hop in its purest mode: a hazy, late-night groove built around murky low end and drifting keys, with That Boy Hi Hat rapping like he's working through something he can't quite name. The title is doing real work — the pain here isn't dramatized, it's smothered and slow-burning, the kind you sit with at 3 a.m. Production stays skeletal on purpose: the space between the drums carries the mood, and his flow fills it with introspective, low-register writing that favors atmosphere over acrobatics. There's a melancholic weight to the record that separates it from the more triumphant post trap entries in the catalog; it's one of his most honest-sounding performances, and its underground status suits it — this isn't a song chasing playlists. It's That Boy Hi Hat at his most nocturnal, letting a song smolder rather than explode. For listeners who came through the bigger singles, 'Smokin' Pain' is the reward for digging: a dark, inward-facing track that proves the alternative rap lane has rooms the singles never enter.

entries.title: Phantasm
entries.source_text:
Phantasm — That Boy Hi Hat
Genres: alternative rap, alt rap, post trap, rap, cyberpunk
'Phantasm' is where That Boy Hi Hat's post-trap futurism goes full neon-noir. A deep cut from Idol or Icon (2021), the track rides an 88 BPM pulse through flickering synths and sub-bass pressure that evokes a city at night rendered in neon — dystopian but magnetic, the sound of a future you can't look away from. His delivery is cool and coiled, riding the beat rather than fighting it, which makes the record hypnotic: it pulls you into its circuitry and holds you there. Behind the scenes, the production history tells its own story — the vault's alternate master was running hot with true-peak clipping, and a September 2026 limiter pass brought it down to a clean -0.5 dBTP, letting the darkness of the mix breathe without distortion. It's a detail only engineers would hear, but it shows how carefully That Boy Hi Hat's team treats the catalog's sonic margins. In alternative rap terms, 'Phantasm' is a scene-setter rather than a statement piece: futuristic, nocturnal, and deliberately unresolved, the kind of track that soundtracks a drive more than a headline. Within the post trap lane, it's one of his most atmospheric builds — proof that the cyberpunk impulse in his music is an aesthetic commitment, not a costume.

entries.title: Misfits and Hooligans
entries.source_text:
Misfits and Hooligans — That Boy Hi Hat
Genres: alternative rap, alt rap, post trap, rap, underground
At five minutes and forty-nine seconds, 'Misfits and Hooligans' is That Boy Hi Hat's longest record on Spotify — and it earns every second. An Idol or Icon (2021) standout, the track is a sprawling underground hip hop statement built for the outsiders: hard-hitting drums, a bass line that rolls rather than stabs, and a hook designed to be shouted back. That Boy Hi Hat writes the whole thing like a manifesto for the kids who never fit the room, and the length becomes a feature — verses stack into verses, the beat breathes, and the defiant energy compounds rather than dissipates. There's an anthemic quality to it that the catalog's darker cuts don't chase: this is hype as community-building, the sound of a crowd finding each other. The post trap architecture keeps it modern — crisp hi-hats, layered low end — but the spirit is older than that, closer to the raw collectivism of early underground rap crews. For a catalog that leans atmospheric and nocturnal, 'Misfits and Hooligans' is That Boy Hi Hat at his most communal: dangerous in intent, inclusive in invitation. It plays like a set-closer even on record, and it's the clearest evidence that his songwriting scales to ambition when the canvas is wide.

entries.title: Roses over Monaco
entries.source_text:
Roses over Monaco — That Boy Hi Hat
Genres: alternative rap, alt rap, post trap, rap
Closing Idol or Icon (2021), 'Roses over Monaco' is That Boy Hi Hat at his most cinematic — a finale engineered to feel like one. The title alone sets the scene: luxury against the backdrop of the French Riviera at night, opulence as a survival story rather than a flex. Production leans widescreen, with layered synths and a slow-blooming arrangement that lets each section arrive like a scene change, and his flow follows suit — measured, unhurried, carrying the weight of late-night reflection. This is post trap rendered as triumph over adversity: the verses acknowledge the climb without dwelling in the wound, and the hook opens up into something genuinely uplifting. In the alternative rap lane, closers do the heaviest emotional lifting — they're the last word a listener carries — and That Boy Hi Hat treats the responsibility seriously. 'Roses over Monaco' doesn't just end the album; it reframes everything before it as prologue, the dark streets that made the roses necessary. It's one of the catalog's most composed performances: nothing hurried, nothing wasted. When the last note fades, the record has done what a great closer should — left you wanting to run the whole journey back.

entries.title: Broken Hearts Club
entries.source_text:
Broken Hearts Club — That Boy Hi Hat
Genres: alternative rap, alt rap, post trap, rap
'Broken Hearts Club' is one of the loudest things That Boy Hi Hat has ever committed to tape — the mix runs at -9.9 dB mean, the hottest in its vault batch — and the volume is the point. This is a heartbreak record that refuses to whisper: at 110 BPM it moves with the forward pressure of a club track, but the writing is pure vulnerability, a melancholic anthem for anyone who's had to rebuild in public. It belongs to the November NO SKIPS EP, a five-track run alongside 'Golden Diamond,' 'Doves & Diamonds,' 'Zooted Zone,' and 'Shaka Zulu' that earned November Discovery Mode eligibility — a lane designed for records that convert casual listeners into believers. As of early October 2026 it had yet to land on Spotify, which makes its VEVO video the primary window: a visual cut uploaded in September 2026 that carries the track's defiant, anthemic energy straight to camera. That Boy Hi Hat has written sadder songs and harder songs, but few that commit to both at once — the polished mix keeps the loudness from turning ragged, and the hook lands like a promise rather than a complaint. 'Broken Hearts Club' is the sound of turning heartbreak into momentum: bass-heavy, unapologetic, and built for rooms full of people who've been there.

entries.title: Star
entries.source_text:
Star — King Akeem
Genres: rap, hip hop
'Star' is the record that proved King Ahkeem belonged on the marquee. The CWI roster artist broke north of 112,000 plays on this single, and the numbers make sense the moment the hook lands: it's a straight-ahead rap anthem built on self-belief, the kind of track that plays like a coronation. Black co-produced the single — and counts Ahkeem's catalog among his own — and that co-production shows in the record's construction: the beat is sturdy and uncluttered, giving King Ahkeem's voice the full frame, while the hook is engineered for maximum carry. This is hip hop in its celebratory register: triumphant without being smug, hype without being frantic. The verses detail the climb with street-narrative specificity; the chorus turns it into something anthemic, a room full of people saying the title back. As of early October 2026, no clean Spotify match had surfaced for the track, which only sharpens its underground hip hop credentials — 'Star' traveled on momentum and word of mouth rather than algorithmic placement. For listeners mapping the wider CWI universe beyond That Boy Hi Hat, 'Star' is the entry point: King Ahkeem's defining statement, and a reminder that ambition, cleanly produced and honestly delivered, still moves numbers on its own.

entries.title: Full Moon
entries.source_text:
Full Moon — 183 Wilboi
Genres: rap, hip hop, trap
There is a particular kind of rap record that only makes sense after midnight, and "Full Moon" is 183 Wilboi's entry in that canon. Co-produced by Black Lansky, the track sits at the intersection of trap and underground hip hop, built on an atmospheric, layered bed that lets 183 Wilboi's delivery carry the weight. The production breathes: an 808-driven low end, crisp hi-hats ticking like a clock, and a spacious synth wash that earns the title — it sounds like driving under a bright moon with the windows down. Mood-wise, "Full Moon" is nocturnal and introspective without turning soft; there is a hypnotic pull to the hook that rewards repeat listens. 183 Wilboi raps with the confidence of an artist who knows his lane — late-night reflection rendered as street narrative, ambition set against the quiet hours. As the pilot record of the Rock-Rap Night session series, it doubles as a statement of intent for the CWI catalog: polished enough for headphones, raw enough for the block. Clean and direct rather than explicit, it plays anywhere the night runs long. In a catalog full of daylight anthems, "Full Moon" owns the dark.

entries.title: Stunt
entries.source_text:
Stunt — 183 Wilboi
Genres: rap, hip hop
"Stunt" is 183 Wilboi in pure showmanship mode — a hype, aggressive trap cut built for the moment before the night peaks. Co-produced by Black Lansky, the record trades the moonlit introspection of "Full Moon" for something harder: anthemic energy, hard-hitting drums, and a bass-heavy mix designed to rattle a room. 183 Wilboi attacks the track with defiant swagger, the kind of performance that turns a verse into a declaration. The production keeps it lean and mean — underground hip hop with the punch of a catalog centerpiece, crisp hi-hats cutting through the low end and a hook engineered for call-and-response. Currently living as a reference recording in the CWI vault rather than a commercial release, "Stunt" shows the other half of 183 Wilboi's range: not the thinker in the driver's seat, but the headliner commanding the crowd. For fans tracking the Rock-Rap Night sessions, it is the loudest thing in the room, and a clear signal that 183 Wilboi can carry a stage as easily as a session.

entries.title: vai vem vem
entries.source_text:
vai vem vem — Dre50
Jamaican artist Dre50 brings cross-Caribbean heat to the CWI catalog with "vai vem vem," a co-production with Black Lansky that released September 30, 2026. The title — Portuguese for the push and pull of coming and going — sets the tone for a seductive, hypnotic record built for late-night dancefloors. Dre50 rides the beat with the fluidity of an artist fluent in island rhythm, and the production answers with an 808-driven groove that sits comfortably in the underground hip hop lane, trap drums anchoring the sway. There is a dangerous charm to "vai vem vem": seductive on the surface, loaded with street narrative underneath. The polished mix keeps every element crisp — the percussion, the low end, Dre50's commanding vocal presence. Released under Cumulative Web Inc, it marks Dre50 as one of the roster's most internationally flavored voices, a bridge between Kingston energy and the CWI sound. "vai vem vem" does not chase trends; it sets a mood and holds it.

entries.title: Pay Yourself
entries.source_text:
Pay Yourself — Greg Porn
Genres: rap, hip hop, underground
"Pay Yourself" is Greg Porn's money manifesto — a defiant, aggressive underground hip hop cut that treats self-belief as a business plan. DistroKid-verified and released under Cumulative Web Inc, the track finds Greg Porn in full triumph-over-adversity mode, a triumphant, defiant energy, rapping like a man who has decided that nobody is coming to save him, and that is fine. The production is bass-heavy and hard-hitting, trap drums punching beneath a lean, menacing arrangement that leaves the vocal nowhere to hide — which is exactly where Greg Porn wants it. Explicit and unapologetic, "Pay Yourself" builds its hook around ambition as discipline: the title is both a command and a philosophy. Within the CWI catalog, it sits alongside the roster's hardest underground records, a street narrative that doubles as financial advice. Greg Porn's delivery is all conviction — no wasted bars, no borrowed energy. This is the sound of an artist paying himself first and daring the industry to keep up.

entries.title: On Edge
entries.source_text:
On Edge — Greg Porn
Genres: rap, hip hop, underground
"On Edge" finds Greg Porn leaning into tension — a dangerous, late-night underground hip hop record that lives up to its title. DistroKid-verified under Cumulative Web Inc, the track trades anthem-sized hooks for something more wire-taut: atmospheric production, crisp hi-hats, and a vocal performance that sounds one bar away from snapping. Greg Porn raps with an introspective edge here, turning street narrative inward — the paranoia and pressure that come with ambition, rendered without flinching. The mix is lean and menacing, an 808-driven low end pressing against a sparse, nocturnal arrangement, with trap drums that hit like a pulse running too fast. Within Greg Porn's CWI run — alongside "Pay Yourself" and the unreleased "Unholy Hunter" — "On Edge" is the uneasy middle chapter: aggressive but controlled, hypnotic but never comfortable. It is the sound of an artist who knows exactly how close to the line he is standing, and keeps walking anyway.

entries.title: Unholy Hunter
entries.source_text:
Unholy Hunter — Greg Porn
Genres: rap, hip hop, underground
"Unholy Hunter" is Greg Porn at his darkest — and right now it exists only as a two-minute reference statement, Ref 1.0, awaiting its final mix and artist clearance. What the reference already makes clear: this is dystopian, aggressive underground hip hop, a dangerous record whose title does its own forecasting. Greg Porn stalks the beat with predatory confidence, and somewhere in the run there is a shout-out to Black Lansky — a reminder that the CWI machine is in the room even when the track is at its most feral. The raw reference form only sharpens the effect: no polish to blunt the edges, just nocturnal menace and a trap-leaning, bass-heavy low end that feels like pursuit. When the final mix lands, "Unholy Hunter" will sit as the darkest chapter in Greg Porn's catalog run — the companion piece to "Pay Yourself"'s discipline and "On Edge"'s tension. For now, it is a two-minute warning shot from an artist hunting at full throttle.

entries.title: 2K23 Corner$
entries.source_text:
2K23 Corner$ — Fleekz
Genres: rap, hip hop, underground
Released February 7, 2023 as a single, "2K23 Corner$" pairs Fleekz with That Boy Hi Hat for a dangerous, aggressive underground hip hop cut straight from the street-narrative playbook. Fleekz sets the tone with hungry, hard-hitting delivery over trap drums and a bass-heavy mix; then That Boy Hi Hat slides in and reminds you why his "Appears On" section is worth checking — a feature verse that treats the corner as both setting and state of mind. The production is lean and menacing: crisp hi-hats, an 808-driven low end, and an atmospheric edge that keeps the record nocturnal without losing its daytime punch. Explicit and unapologetic, "2K23 Corner$" is a time capsule of the 2023 underground and a key early link between That Boy Hi Hat and the wider CWI orbit — the kind of collaboration that foreshadows a catalog. For That Boy Hi Hat completists, it is an essential feature; for Fleekz, it is the calling card.

entries.title: Cyberpunk 2027
entries.source_text:
Cyberpunk 2027 — That Boy Hi Hat
Genres: alternative rap, alt rap, post trap, rap
Moods: dark, cinematic, futuristic, nocturnal, dystopian
Out October 20, 2026, "Cyberpunk 2027" is That Boy Hi Hat's flagship single — and the most ambitious record in the CWI catalog to date. Produced by Kokurcho, the two-time Billboard-charting, BET Awards-nominated producer behind records for Lil Durk, GloRilla, and Duwap Kaine, and executive co-produced by Black Lansky, the track was recorded at Cue Recording Studios in Falls Church, VA, and it sounds like the budget: cinematic production on a widescreen scale. This is alternative rap as blockbuster — synth-heavy and synth-driven, layered and atmospheric, with an 808-driven undercurrent that keeps the future rooted in the streets. That Boy Hi Hat has never sounded more commanding. He moves through the dystopian landscape the track builds — neon-noir imagery, urban decay, a future that feels twelve months away rather than twelve years — with the poise of an artist who invented the lane. The mood is dark, cinematic, futuristic, and unapologetically dystopian; the hook lands like a transmission from the world the title names. As the anchor of That Boy Hi Hat's post-trap futurism era and the lead single of the Cyberpunk 2027 campaign, this is the record everything else in the catalog points toward: alt rap elevated to cinema. The future, per That Boy Hi Hat, is already here — and it knocks.
